claim: Neutral events preceding emotional experiences can be better remembered.
source: Neutral events preceding emotional experiences can be better remembered, likely by assigning them as significant to guide possible use in future.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general premise of the study.

claim: The neurobiological mechanisms of how emotional learning enhances memory for past mundane events remain unclear.
source: Yet, the neurobiological mechanisms of how emotional learning enhances memory for past mundane events remain unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract.

claim: Emotional learning retroactively enhanced initial memory for neutral associations across three studies.
source: Behaviorally, emotional learning retroactively enhanced initial memory for neutral associations across the three studies.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data from Studies 1, 2, and 3.

claim: Emotional learning potentiated trial-specific reactivation of overlapping neural traces in the hippocampus and stimulus-relevant neocortex.
source: Neurally, emotional learning potentiated trial-specific reactivation of overlapping neural traces in the hippocampus and stimulus-relevant neocortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by fMRI data from Study 3.

claim: Emotional learning induced rapid hippocampal-neocortical functional reorganization supporting retroactive memory benefit.
source: It further induced rapid hippocampal-neocortical functional reorganization supporting such retroactive memory benefit, as characterized by enhanced hippocampal-neocortical coupling modulated by the amygdala during emotional learning, and a shift of hippocampal connectivity from stimulus-relevant neocortex to distributed transmodal prefrontal-parietal areas at post-learning rests.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by connectivity analyses from Study 3.

claim: Experiencing an emotional event often strengthens memory for the event itself and can benefit memories for other mundane events occurring separately in time.
source: Experiencing an emotional event such as a psychological trauma, for instance, often not only strengthens our memory for the event itself, but also can benefit memories for other mundane events occurring separately in time (LaBar and Cabeza, 2006; Li et al., 2008; Wong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There has been substantial progress in understanding the mechanisms underlying memory enhancement for emotional events themselves.
source: There has been substantial progress in understanding the mechanisms underlying memory enhancement for emotional events themselves, owing to autonomic reactions to emotional arousal that stimulates the encoding and post-encoding processes of emotional memory (Hamann, 2001; LaBar and Cabeza, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Human episodic memory is theorized to organize experiences into a highly adaptive network of integrated representations that can be prioritized based on the significance of preceding or following events.
source: Since we cannot determine which event will become significant later, human episodic memory is theorized to organize our experiences into a highly adaptive network of integrated representations, that can be prioritized in terms of the significance of preceding or following events (Ritchey et al., 2016; Shohamy and Daw, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical frameworks in the literature.

claim: The retroactive effect may lead to maladaptive generalization recognized as a cognitive hallmark of core symptoms in PTSD and phobia.
source: However, this retroactive effect may also lead to maladaptive generalization recognized as a cognitive hallmark of core symptoms in some mental disorders, like posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and phobia (Lange et al., 2019; Mary et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on mental disorders.

claim: Studies of behavioral tagging have provided evidence for delayed retroactive memory enhancement following a strongly salient or emotional experience.
source: Studies of the behavioral tagging have provided prominent evidence for the delayed retroactive memory enhancement following a strongly salient or emotional experience, typically resulting in a generalized form of enhancement on initial weak memories encoded closely in time (Ballarini et al., 2009; Dunsmoor et al., 2022; Takeuchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous behavioral tagging studies.

claim: Animal work has shown that a salient stimulus can spread its value to an indirect neutral event through an integration mechanism.
source: Animal work has shown that the salient stimulus can spread its value to the indirect neutral event through an integration mechanism (Holmes et al., 2018; Sadacca et al., 2018; Sharpe et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: Human studies have suggested that a subsequent salient event could enhance perceptual discrimination and guide decision bias for its related neutral events.
source: Human studies have also suggested that a subsequent salient event could enhance perceptual discrimination and guide decision bias for its related neutral events (Kuhl et al., 2010; Li et al., 2008; Wimmer and Shohamy, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human studies.

claim: As new emotional experiences are encoded, related memories for past sensory events can be reactivated and integrated with the emotional memory content, resulting in a retroactive memory benefit.
source: Recent memory integration views of sensory preconditioning paradigm posit that, as new emotional experiences are encoded, related memories for past sensory (neutral) events can be reactivated and integrated with the emotional memory content, essentially resulting in a retroactive memory benefit (Holmes et al., 2022; Schlichting and Frankland, 2017; Shohamy and Daw, 2015; Wong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to memory integration theories.

claim: Human neuroimaging studies provide evidence that a newly encoded event can be updated and reorganized into relevant episodic memory through reactivation of overlapping neural ensembles engaged in both initial and new learning.
source: Human neuroimaging studies provide compelling evidence supporting the integrative encoding mechanism, by which a newly encoded event can be updated and reorganized into relevant episodic memory through reactivation of overlapping neural ensembles engaged in both initial and new learning (Schlichting and Preston, 2015; Shohamy and Wagner, 2008; van Kesteren et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: The hippocampus serves as an integrative hub by binding disparate representations in stimulus-sensitive neocortical areas into episodic memories.
source: The hippocampus serves as an integrative hub by binding disparate representations in stimulus-sensitive neocortical areas into episodic memories (Kuhl et al., 2010; van Kesteren et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on hippocampal function.

claim: Reactivation of hippocampal and stimulus-sensitive neocortical representations has been proposed to promote systems-level memory integration.
source: Reactivation of hippocampal and stimulus-sensitive neocortical representations has been well proposed to promote systems-level memory integration (Schlichting and Preston, 2014; Sutherland and McNaughton, 2000; Zhuang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on memory integration.

claim: Emotional arousal can lead to better episodic memory through strengthening hippocampal connectivity with the amygdala and related neocortical regions during emotional memory encoding.
source: Many studies have suggested that emotional arousal can lead to better episodic memory through strengthening hippocampal connectivity with the amygdala and related neocortical regions during emotional memory encoding (Dolcos et al., 2004; Hermans et al., 2014; Richardson et al., 2004; Ritchey et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on emotional memory.

claim: Offline processes at awake rest and sleep contribute to emotional memory benefit, likely involving reconfiguration of hippocampal functional connectivity with distributed neocortical networks.
source: Beyond online encoding, offline processes at awake rest and sleep also contribute to emotional memory benefit, most likely involving reconfiguration of hippocampal functional connectivity with distributed neocortical networks (de Voogd et al., 2016; Schlichting and Frankland, 2017; Tambini et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on offline memory consolidation.

claim: Neural engagement prior to encoding could affect the allocation of new information into specific neural populations and form a preparatory network for memory integration.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated that neural engagement, for instance, excitable hippocampal-neocortical coordinated interactions prior to encoding could affect the allocation of new information into specific neural populations and form a preparatory network for igniting reactivation or replay cascades to support memory integration (Josselyn and Frankland, 2018; Kaefer et al., 2022; Schlichting and Frankland, 2017; van Dongen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies on neural preparatory states.

claim: In Study 1, 30 participants learned 72 neutral face-object pairs during the initial learning phase.
source: In Study 1 (N=30), participants learnt 72 neutral face-object pairs during the initial learning phase.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Study 1.

claim: In Study 1, each face from the initial learning phase was paired with either an aversive screaming voice or a neutral voice during the emotional learning phase.
source: Thereafter, each face from the initial learning phase was presented as a cue and paired with either an aversive screaming voice (i.e. aversive condition) or a neutral voice (i.e. neutral condition) during the emotional learning phase.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Study 1.

claim: In Study 1, a surprise associative memory test was administered 30 min after the emotional learning phase.
source: A surprise associative memory test was administered 30 min later to assess memory performance for initial face-object associations.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Study 1.

claim: In Study 2, the reproducibility of Study 1 was examined by another independent research group.
source: In Study 2 (N=28), the reproducibility of Study 1 was examined by another independent research group.
evidence: This describes the purpose of Study 2.

claim: In Study 3, participants underwent fMRI scanning during the initial and emotional learning phases that were interleaved by three rest scans.
source: In Study 3 (N=28), participants underwent fMRI scanning during the initial and emotional learning phases that were interleaved by three rest scans, with concurrent skin conductance recording to monitor autonomic arousal.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Study 3.

claim: In Study 1, there was a main effect of Emotion on associative memory performance (F(1,29) = 5.18, p=0.030, partial η2=0.15).
source: For Study 1, this analysis revealed main effects of Emotion (F(1,29) = 5.18, p=0.030, partial η2=0.15) and Confidence (F(1,29) = 142.07, p<0.001, partial η2=0.83; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Study 1 shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In Study 1, there was a main effect of Confidence on associative memory performance (F(1,29) = 142.07, p<0.001, partial η2=0.83).
source: For Study 1, this analysis revealed main effects of Emotion (F(1,29) = 5.18, p=0.030, partial η2=0.15) and Confidence (F(1,29) = 142.07, p<0.001, partial η2=0.83; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Study 1 shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In Study 1, post-hoc comparisons revealed better memory for face-object associations with high confidence in the aversive than neutral condition (t(29) = 2.18, p=0.037, dav = 0.22).
source: Post-hoc comparisons revealed better memory for face-object associations only with high confidence in the aversive than neutral condition (t(29) = 2.18, p=0.037, dav = 0.22), but not with low confidence (t(29) = –0.15, p=0.883).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc analysis in Study 1.

claim: In Study 2, there was a main effect of Emotion on associative memory performance (F(1,27) = 5.53, p=0.026, partial η2=0.17).
source: Parallel analysis in Study 2 also revealed main effects of Emotion (F(1,27) = 5.53, p=0.026, partial η2=0.17) and Confidence (F(1,27) = 206.14, p<0.001, partial η2=0.88), and a significant Emotion-by-Confidence interaction (F(1,27) = 4.94, p=0.035, partial η2=0.16; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Study 2 shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In Study 2, there was a significant Emotion-by-Confidence interaction on associative memory performance (F(1,27) = 4.94, p=0.035, partial η2=0.16).
source: Parallel analysis in Study 2 also revealed main effects of Emotion (F(1,27) = 5.53, p=0.026, partial η2=0.17) and Confidence (F(1,27) = 206.14, p<0.001, partial η2=0.88), and a significant Emotion-by-Confidence interaction (F(1,27) = 4.94, p=0.035, partial η2=0.16; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Study 2 shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In Study 2, post-hoc comparisons revealed better associative memory with high confidence in the aversive condition compared to neutral condition (t(27) = 2.47, p=0.020, dav = 0.23).
source: Post-hoc comparisons also revealed better associative memory with high confidence in the aversive (vs. neutral) condition (t(27) = 2.47, p=0.020, dav = 0.23), but not with low confidence (t(27) = –0.55, p=0.588).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc analysis in Study 2.

claim: In Study 3, there was a main effect of Confidence on associative memory performance (F(1,27) = 29.35, p<0.001, partial η2=0.52).
source: In Study 3 (fMRI), we again observed a similar pattern of results, including the main effect of Confidence (F(1,27) = 29.35, p<0.001, partial η2=0.52) and the significant Emotion-by-Confidence interaction (F(1,27) = 8.61, p=0.007, partial η2=0.24; Figure 1D)
evidence: This is a statistical result from Study 3 shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In Study 3, there was a significant Emotion-by-Confidence interaction on associative memory performance (F(1,27) = 8.61, p=0.007, partial η2=0.24).
source: In Study 3 (fMRI), we again observed a similar pattern of results, including the main effect of Confidence (F(1,27) = 29.35, p<0.001, partial η2=0.52) and the significant Emotion-by-Confidence interaction (F(1,27) = 8.61, p=0.007, partial η2=0.24; Figure 1D)
evidence: This is a statistical result from Study 3 shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In Study 3, there was a retroactive enhancement on associative memory with high confidence in the aversive condition compared to neutral condition (t(27) = 2.59, p=0.015, dav = 0.10).
source: specifically with a retroactive enhancement on associative memory with high confidence in the aversive (vs. neutral) condition (t(27) = 2.59, p=0.015, dav = 0.10), but an opposite effect for associations with low confidence (t(27) = –2.18, p=0.038, dav = 0.24).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc analysis in Study 3.

claim: Vividness ratings during initial learning were significantly positively correlated with confidence ratings during memory test across three studies.
source: This analysis revealed significantly positive but moderate correlations between vividness ratings (i.e. a four-point scale: 4 = 'Very vivid', 1 = 'Not vivid at all') and confidence ratings across three studies (Study 1: β=0.15, p<0.001, 95% CI = [0.07, 0.22]; Study 2: β=0.13, p<0.001, 95% CI = [0.07, 0.19]; Study 3: β=0.24, p<0.001, 95% CI = [0.16, 0.32]; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a statistical result from linear mixed-effects model analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: In Study 1, there was significantly better memory in the aversive condition compared to neutral condition for high-vividness encoded associations (t(29) = 2.15, p=0.040, dav = 0.21).
source: Separate paired t-tests for the three studies revealed significantly better memory in the aversive (vs. neutral) condition, selectively for high-vividness encoded associations (Study 1: t(29) = 2.15, p=0.040, dav = 0.21; Study 2: t(27) = 2.16, p=0.040, dav = 0.25; Study 3: t(27) = 2.21, p=0.036, dav = 0.12)
evidence: This is a statistical result from paired t-test in Study 1.

claim: In Study 2, there was significantly better memory in the aversive condition compared to neutral condition for high-vividness encoded associations (t(27) = 2.16, p=0.040, dav = 0.25).
source: Separate paired t-tests for the three studies revealed significantly better memory in the aversive (vs. neutral) condition, selectively for high-vividness encoded associations (Study 1: t(29) = 2.15, p=0.040, dav = 0.21; Study 2: t(27) = 2.16, p=0.040, dav = 0.25; Study 3: t(27) = 2.21, p=0.036, dav = 0.12)
evidence: This is a statistical result from paired t-test in Study 2.

claim: In Study 3, there was significantly better memory in the aversive condition compared to neutral condition for high-vividness encoded associations (t(27) = 2.21, p=0.036, dav = 0.12).
source: Separate paired t-tests for the three studies revealed significantly better memory in the aversive (vs. neutral) condition, selectively for high-vividness encoded associations (Study 1: t(29) = 2.15, p=0.040, dav = 0.21; Study 2: t(27) = 2.16, p=0.040, dav = 0.25; Study 3: t(27) = 2.21, p=0.036, dav = 0.12)
evidence: This is a statistical result from paired t-test in Study 3.

claim: In Study 3, there was significantly higher skin conductance level in the aversive than neutral condition during the emotional learning phase (t(19) = 2.23, p=0.038, dav = 0.50).
source: Post-hoc comparisons revealed significantly higher SCL in the aversive than neutral condition during the emotional learning phase (t(19) = 2.23, p=0.038, dav = 0.50), but not during the initial learning phase (t(19) = –1.16, p=0.26).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparison of skin conductance data in Study 3.

claim: Emotional learning induced a general increase in reactivation of initial learning activity in the hippocampus, vLOC, and FFA.
source: These analyses revealed a general emotion-induced increase in reactivation of initial learning activity in the hippocampus and stimulus-sensitive vLOC and FFA (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2 for statistics).
evidence: This is a finding from condition-level pattern similarity analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was a significant main effect of Emotion on hippocampal pattern similarity (F(1, 25)=9.48, p=0.005, partial η2=0.28).
source: These analyses revealed significant main effects of Emotion in the hippocampus (F(1, 25)=9.48, p=0.005, partial η2=0.28) and vLOC (F(1, 25)=9.34, p=0.005, partial η2=0.27)
evidence: This is a statistical result from trial-level pattern similarity analysis.

claim: There was a significant main effect of Emotion on vLOC pattern similarity (F(1, 25)=9.34, p=0.005, partial η2=0.27).
source: These analyses revealed significant main effects of Emotion in the hippocampus (F(1, 25)=9.48, p=0.005, partial η2=0.28) and vLOC (F(1, 25)=9.34, p=0.005, partial η2=0.27)
evidence: This is a statistical result from trial-level pattern similarity analysis.

claim: There was a significant Emotion-by-Measure interaction effect on hippocampal pattern similarity (F(1, 25)=4.89, p=0.036, partial η2=0.16).
source: as well as a significant Emotion-by-Measure interaction effect in the hippocampus (F(1, 25)=4.89, p=0.036, partial η2=0.16) and a similar trend but non-significant interaction in the vLOC (F(1, 25)=3.54, p=0.072, partial η2=0.12)
evidence: This is a statistical result from trial-level pattern similarity analysis.

claim: Post-hoc comparisons revealed significantly higher pair-specific similarity in hippocampus in the aversive than neutral condition (F(1, 25)=7.24, p=0.013, partial η2=0.22).
source: Post-hoc comparisons (with covariates controlled) revealed significantly higher pair-specific similarity in both hippocampus (F(1, 25)=7.24, p=0.013, partial η2=0.22) and vLOC (F(1, 25)=8.28, p=0.008, partial η2=0.25) in the aversive than neutral condition.
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparison of pattern similarity.

claim: Post-hoc comparisons revealed significantly higher pair-specific similarity in vLOC in the aversive than neutral condition (F(1, 25)=8.28, p=0.008, partial η2=0.25).
source: Post-hoc comparisons (with covariates controlled) revealed significantly higher pair-specific similarity in both hippocampus (F(1, 25)=7.24, p=0.013, partial η2=0.22) and vLOC (F(1, 25)=8.28, p=0.008, partial η2=0.25) in the aversive than neutral condition.
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparison of pattern similarity.

claim: Hippocampal pair-specific similarity positively predicted memory in the aversive condition (r(predicted, observed)=0.46, p=0.008).
source: These analyses revealed that hippocampal pair-specific similarity positively predicted memory in the aversive (r(predicted, observed)=0.46, p=0.008) but not neutral condition (r(predicted, observed)=–0.09, p=0.480; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a result from machine learning-based prediction analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There was a significant difference in correlation coefficients between aversive and neutral conditions for hippocampal pair-specific similarity predicting memory (z=2.54, p=0.011).
source: Further Steiger's test (Steiger, 1980) revealed a significant difference in correlation coefficients between aversive and neutral conditions (z=2.54, p=0.011).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Steiger's test comparing correlation coefficients.

claim: Hippocampal across-pair similarity positively predicted memory in both aversive (r(predicted, observed)=0.43, p=0.014) and neutral (r(predicted, observed)=0.50, p=0.001) conditions.
source: Hippocampal across-pair similarity positively predicted memory in both aversive (r(predicted, observed)=0.43, p=0.014) and neutral (r(predicted, observed)=0.50, p=0.001) conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A)
evidence: This is a result from machine learning-based prediction analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Emotional learning induced greater functional coupling of the hippocampus with the right amygdala, left mFFA, and left sLOC in the aversive compared to neutral condition.
source: In line with our priori hypothesis, we mainly focused on significant clusters in the right amygdala (Figure 3B), left middle portion of FFA (mFFA; Figure 3C) and left superior portion of LOC (sLOC; Figure 3D), which showed greater functional coupling with the hippocampus in the aversive (vs. neutral) condition during emotional learning
evidence: This is a finding from task-dependent PPI analysis shown in Figures 3B-D.

claim: There were significant main effects of Memory on hippocampal connectivity with mFFA (F(1, 26)=5.59, p=0.026, partial η2=0.18) and sLOC (F(1, 26)=4.40, p=0.046, partial η2=0.15).
source: This analysis revealed significant main effects of Memory in hippocampal connectivity with the mFFA (F(1, 26)=5.59, p=0.026, partial η2=0.18; Figure 3F) and sLOC (F(1, 26)=4.40, p=0.046, partial η2=0.15; Figure 3G), but not in hippocampal-amygdala connectivity (F(1, 26)=0.21, p=0.65, partial η2=0.008; Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a statistical result from ANOVA on hippocampal connectivity shown in Figures 3E-G.

claim: Greater hippocampal connectivity with mFFA predicted better associative memory in the aversive condition (r(predicted, observed)=0.57, p<0.001).
source: Interestingly, we found that greater hippocampal connectivity with mFFA and sLOC (i.e. remembered with high confidence relative to forgotten) were predictive of better associative memory (i.e. remembered with high confidence) in the aversive condition (mFFA: r(predicted, observed)=0.57, p<0.001; sLOC: r(predicted, observed)=0.65, p<0.001; Figure 3H–J)
evidence: This is a result from machine learning-based prediction analysis shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Greater hippocampal connectivity with sLOC predicted better associative memory in the aversive condition (r(predicted, observed)=0.65, p<0.001).
source: Interestingly, we found that greater hippocampal connectivity with mFFA and sLOC (i.e. remembered with high confidence relative to forgotten) were predictive of better associative memory (i.e. remembered with high confidence) in the aversive condition (mFFA: r(predicted, observed)=0.57, p<0.001; sLOC: r(predicted, observed)=0.65, p<0.001; Figure 3H–J)
evidence: This is a result from machine learning-based prediction analysis shown in Figure 3J.

claim: There were significant differences in correlation coefficients between aversive and neutral conditions for hippocampal coupling with mFFA (z=2.13, p=0.033) and sLOC (z=2.15, p=0.032).
source: Further Steiger's tests revealed significant differences in correlation coefficients between two conditions for hippocampal coupling with mFFA (z=2.13, p=0.033) and sLOC (z=2.15, p=0.032), and a non-significant trend of difference for hippocampal-amygdala coupling (z=1.79, p=0.073).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Steiger's test comparing correlation coefficients.

claim: Hippocampal-mFFA and -sLOC connectivity mediated the influence of hippocampal-amygdala connectivity on associative memory performance in the aversive condition (Indirect Est = 0.19, p=0.010, 95% CI = [0.044, 0.328]).
source: This exploratory mediation analysis revealed two significant mediating effects on the positive relationship between hippocampal-amygdala connectivity and memory outcome (hippocampal couplings with mFFA and sLOC: Indirect Est = 0.19, p=0.010, 95% CI = [0.044, 0.328], and hippocampal–sLOC coupling: Indirect Est = 0.20, p=0.016, 95% CI = [0.036, 0.360]).
evidence: This is a result from exploratory mediation analysis.

claim: Hippocampal-sLOC connectivity mediated the influence of hippocampal-amygdala connectivity on associative memory performance in the aversive condition (Indirect Est = 0.20, p=0.016, 95% CI = [0.036, 0.360]).
source: This exploratory mediation analysis revealed two significant mediating effects on the positive relationship between hippocampal-amygdala connectivity and memory outcome (hippocampal couplings with mFFA and sLOC: Indirect Est = 0.19, p=0.010, 95% CI = [0.044, 0.328], and hippocampal–sLOC coupling: Indirect Est = 0.20, p=0.016, 95% CI = [0.036, 0.360]).
evidence: This is a result from exploratory mediation analysis.

claim: Hippocampal-iLOC connectivity at post-initial-learning rest positively correlated with associative memory in the aversive condition.
source: Specifically, the exploratory whole-brain analyses revealed that hippocampal-iLOC connectivity at post-initial-learning rest positively correlated with associative memory in the aversive condition, but negatively correlated with memory in the neutral condition (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1A for visualization).
evidence: This is a finding from exploratory whole-brain connectivity analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Hippocampal connectivity with transmodal prefrontal-parietal regions at post-emotional-learning rest positively correlated with memory in the aversive condition.
source: We also observed that hippocampal connectivity with transmodal prefrontal-parietal regions (i.e. IPL, PCC, aPFC and mPFC) at post-emotional-learning rest positively correlated with memory in the aversive condition, but negatively in the neutral condition (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1B for visualization).
evidence: This is a finding from exploratory whole-brain connectivity analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Machine learning-based prediction analyses revealed positive predictions for associative memory in the aversive condition for hippocampal connectivity with iLOC (r(predicted, observed)=0.47, p<0.005), IPL (r(predicted, observed)=0.54, p<0.005), PCC (r(predicted, observed)=0.51, p<0.005), aPFC (r(predicted, observed)=0.52, p<0.005), and mPFC (r(predicted, observed)=0.48, p<0.005).
source: As a complement, the machine learning-based prediction analyses for post-learning hippocampal connectivity changes revealed very similar patterns of positive predictions for associative memory in the aversive condition (iLOC: r(predicted, observed)=0.47; IPL: r(predicted, observed)=0.54; PCC: r(predicted, observed)=0.51; aPFC: r(predicted, observed)=0.52; mPFC: r(predicted, observed)=0.48; all p<0.005 while controlling for memory in the neutral condition)
evidence: This is a result from machine learning-based prediction analysis.

claim: The task-unrelated parahippocampal connectivity analysis revealed no reliable clusters for emotion-charged retroactive memory benefit.
source: The control analyses revealed no reliable clusters survived for the task-unrelated parahippocampal connectivity during post-learning rests in relation with emotion-charged retroactive memory benefit (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a result from control connectivity analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The emotion-charged retroactive memory benefit differs from conventional behavioral tagging effects by allowing investigation of trial-specific enhancement through associative learning tasks.
source: First, such sensory preconditioning paradigm allows us to investigate trial-specific enhancement for each pair by associative learning task (Wang and Kahnt, 2021; Wimmer and Shohamy, 2012), in which the overlapping face cues were presented during both initial and emotional learning phases, rather than a general effect with non-overlapping stimuli in each phase (Clewett et al., 2022; Dunsmoor et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a discussion point comparing the current paradigm to behavioral tagging, supported by citations.

claim: The observed retroactive memory enhancement occurred in the immediate test, differing from the delayed benefit in behavioral tagging literature.
source: Second, consistent with the sensory preconditioning models (Kurth-Nelson et al., 2015; Sharpe et al., 2017), we observed the retroactive memory enhancement in the immediate test, which differs from the delayed benefit pertaining to behavioral tagging literature (Ballarini et al., 2009; Dunsmoor et al., 2012; Dunsmoor et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a discussion point comparing the current findings to behavioral tagging, supported by citations.

claim: The observed retroactive benefit was selective for strongly encoded associations, contradicting the rescued effect for initial weak memories expected by behavioral tagging models.
source: Third, our observed retroactive benefit was selective for strongly encoded associations as indicated by high-vividness ratings (presumably strong memories)(Holmes et al., 2022), which contradicts with the rescued effect for initial weak memories expected by behavioral tagging models (Dunsmoor et al., 2015; Ritchey et al., 2016; ).
evidence: This is a discussion point comparing the current findings to behavioral tagging, supported by citations.

claim: A total of 89 young, healthy college students participated in three separate studies.
source: A total of 89 young, healthy college students participated in three separate studies.
evidence: This describes the total sample across all studies.

claim: In Study 1, 30 participants (16 females; mean age ±s.d., 22.23±2.05 years old, ranged from 18 to 26 years) were recruited from Beijing area.
source: In Study 1, 30 participants (16 females; mean age ±s.d., 22.23±2.05 years old, ranged from 18 to 26 years) were recruited from Beijing area to participate in a behavioral experiment.
evidence: This describes the sample characteristics for Study 1.

claim: In Study 2, 28 participants (14 females; mean age ±s.d., 21.83±1.93 years old, ranged from 18 to 26 years) were recruited from Xinyang city in Henan province.
source: In Study 2 by an independent research staff, 28 participants (14 females; mean age ±s.d., 21.83±1.93 years old, ranged from 18 to 26 years) were recruited from Xinyang city in Henan province for a replication experiment to ensure the reliability of our behavioral findings from Study 1.
evidence: This describes the sample characteristics for Study 2.

claim: In Study 3, 31 participants (17 females; mean age ±s.d., 22.55±2.25 years old, ranged from 18 to 27 years) were recruited from Beijing area, with 3 excluded from analysis.
source: In Study 3, another independent cohort of 31 participants (17 females; mean age ±s.d., 22.55±2.25 years old, ranged from 18 to 27 years) was recruited from Beijing area to participate in an event-related fMRI experiment. Data from three participants were excluded from further analyses due to either falling asleep during fMRI scanning (n=2) or poor memory performance (i.e. the overall memory accuracy across confidence ratings and conditions was almost 0; n=1).
evidence: This describes the sample characteristics and exclusions for Study 3.

claim: One hundred and forty-four face images (72 males and 72 females) were selected from a database with color photographs of Chinese individuals.
source: One hundred and forty-four face images (72 males and 72 females) were carefully selected from a database with color photographs of Chinese individuals unknown to participants (Chen et al., 2012), under following criteria suggested by previous studies: direct gaze contact, no headdress, no glasses, no beard, etc (Qin et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the materials used in the study, with citations to the source database and selection criteria.

claim: Seventy-two object images were obtained from a website or publicly available resources on the internet.
source: Seventy-two object images were obtained from a website (http://www.lifeonwhite.com) or publicly available resources on the internet (Dunsmoor et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the materials used in the study, with citation to a previous study.

claim: Four short clips of female voices were selected, with two aversive screams and two neutral voices.
source: Four short clips of female voices were carefully selected from an audio source website (https://www.smzy.com/), with two aversive screams serving as emotional arousal manipulation and two neutral voices (i.e. 'Ah' and 'Eh') as control.
evidence: This describes the auditory stimuli used in the study.

claim: In a pilot experiment, two aversive screams had significantly higher arousal and lower valence than neutral voices (all p<0.001).
source: Two aversive screams had significantly higher arousal and lower valence than neutral voices (all p<0.001; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from a pilot experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: During initial learning, participants were instructed to vividly imagine each face and its paired object interacting with each other.
source: To ensure incidental memory encoding, participants were instructed to vividly imagine each face interacting with its paired object and give a vividness rating on their imagined scenario on a 4-point Likert scale (i.e. 4 = 'Very vivid', 1 = 'Not vivid at all').
evidence: This describes the task instructions for the initial learning phase.

claim: During emotional learning, each face from initial learning was presented for 2 s, then followed by concurrent presentation of the same face paired with either an aversive or a neutral voice for another 2 s.
source: During emotional learning, each face from initial learning was presented at the center of screen for 2 s, and then followed by concurrent presentation of the same face paired with either an aversive or a neutral voice for another 2 s.
evidence: This describes the timing and structure of the emotional learning phase.

claim: The bilateral hippocampal, bilateral vLOC and bilateral FFA ROIs were functionally identified by the overlapping area of two activation contrasts of face-object initial encoding and face-voice emotional encoding relative to fixation.
source: The bilateral hippocampal, bilateral ventral LOC (vLOC) and bilateral FFA ROIs were functionally identified by the overlapping area of two activation contrasts of face-object initial encoding and face-voice emotional encoding relative to fixation (i.e. all encoding trials vs. fixation during each learning phase; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), in order to specify the most engaged regions in both initial and emotional learning (i.e. activated and/or reactivated).
evidence: This describes the method for defining ROIs, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Whole-brain imaging data were collected on a 3T Siemens Prisma MR scanner with a 20-channel head coil system at Peking University in Beijing, China.
source: Whole-brain imaging data were collected on a 3T Siemens Prisma MR scanner (Siemens Medical, Erlangen, Germany) with a 20-channel head coil system at Peking University in Beijing, China.
evidence: This describes the imaging acquisition parameters.

claim: Functional images were collected using a multi-band echo-planar imaging (mb-EPI) sequence with specific parameters.
source: Functional images were collected using a multi-band echo-planar imaging (mb-EPI) sequence (slices, 64; slice thickness, 2 mm; TR, 2000 ms; TE, 30ms; flip angle, 90°; multiband accelerate factor, 2; voxel size, 2×2×2 mm; FOV, 224×224 mm; 240 volumes for each of the three rest scans, 365 and 508 volumes for the initial and emotional learning scans separately).
evidence: This describes the fMRI acquisition parameters.
